title: A Chinese case of fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) with orthostatic tremor:case report and literature review on tremor in FXTAS
case_prompt:
A 67-year-old right-handed farmer was evaluated for an 8-year history of slowly progressive limb tremor. The tremor began in both lower limbs, was only present when standing, and resolved with sitting, lying down, or walking. He had no falls and no gait initiation difficulty. For years he carried a diagnosis of essential tremor but took no therapy. Eighteen months before evaluation he noted worsening tremor and unsteadiness, and 8 months before presentation tremor appeared in both arms, markedly interfering with activities of daily living.

Family history was notable for his younger daughter’s premature ovarian insufficiency and a grandson with autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

On examination, there was a visible tremor of both legs on standing (no tremor when sitting), intention tremor of both hands, mild postural tremor of the arms, and a rest tremor in the left hand. He swayed on Romberg’s test and had difficulty with tandem gait but had normal finger-nose and heel-shin coordination, no rigidity, and no nystagmus. Finger tapping was slow and clumsy bilaterally. Cognitive testing revealed an MMSE of 28/30 and MoCA of 20/30. Muscle strength, sensation, and orthostatic blood pressure were normal.

Routine laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver, kidney, and thyroid function, ceruloplasmin, and homocysteine, were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and nerve conduction studies were unremarkable. Brain MRI showed symmetric T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity in the middle cerebellar peduncles, scattered cerebral white-matter hyperintensities, and mild cerebral and cerebellar atrophy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Essential tremor — “The patient was diagnosed with essential tremor for a long time and he was still functional in daily life without any medical therapy.”  
2. Orthostatic myoclonus — “Unlike OT, the bursts are shorter in duration, non-rhythmic, and irregular … Our patient more likely had OT than OM because of other clinical aspects including the long history of the tremor with function, no fall and without problem of initiating gait.”  
3. Other causes of symptomatic orthostatic tremor — “There is a broad spectrum in differential diagnosis of symptomatic OT, including non-tumoral aqueduct stenosis, chronic relapsing polyradiculoneuropathy, pontine lesions … spinocerebellar ataxia type 2, small cell lung cancer, stiff-person syndrome, Graves’ disease and etc., but rarely considering FXTAS.”  
4. Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome — “T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) brain MRI indicated high intensity signals in the bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles … FXTAS were considered and test for permutation of FMR1 gene was performed…”
